culture.reserves-strategiques.title: Strategic oil reserves: a country's life insurance
culture.reserves-strategiques.hook: Hundreds of millions of barrels sleep under the salt of Texas, in French tanks and in Japan. Born from the 1973 shock, these stocks have been used only six times in fifty years. In 2026, they became a weapon against the Hormuz crisis, and even against the price of diesel.
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.0: After the 1973 embargo, importing countries created the IEA and committed to holding ==at least 90 days of net imports== in stock [1][6].
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.1: These reserves have been used collectively only six times. The biggest operation came in March 2026: ==400 million barrels== in response to the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz [3].
culture.reserves-strategiques.tldr.2: A stock does not replace production: it ==buys time==, is expensive to maintain, and each use leaves the country less protected for the next crisis [11][13].

culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.0: 1973: the day the tap was turned off
Rich countries discover they have no plan if oil stops arriving.

In October 1973, during the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil-producing countries declared an embargo against countries supporting Israel. The price of a barrel went from about $2.90 before the embargo to ==$11.65 in January 1974==: it almost quadrupled [2].

For Europe, Japan and the United States, the shock was twofold. Fuel became expensive and, above all, no one knew how long the shortage would last. Each country fended for itself, which pushed prices even higher.

Importing countries drew a lesson: they needed ==their own stocks, and a conductor== to use them together. On 18 November 1974, they signed the agreement creating the International Energy Agency (IEA), whose first task was to secure oil supplies [1].
The United States went further: in 1975, in direct response to the embargo, it created its own Strategic Petroleum Reserve [9].

The idea is simple. A country that imports its oil controls neither the wells, nor the straits, nor the wars. All it can do is give itself time. A strategic reserve is therefore insurance: you pay every year for a disaster you hope never to face.
Before the embargo, a barrel was worth about $2.90. In January 1974, it was worth $11.65 [2]. Economists call this episode the first oil shock.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.1: The 90-day rule, and how the taps are opened
An IEA country must be able to last at least 90 days without importing oil.

The IEA's basic rule fits in one sentence: each member country must hold stocks equal to ==at least 90 days of its net oil imports== [6]. A country that produces some of its own oil imports less, so it has to store less.

The European Union has its own, stricter rule. Since a 2009 directive, each state must hold the larger of two quantities: ==90 days of net imports or 61 days of domestic consumption==. The obligation had to be met by 31 December 2012 at the latest [5].

Not all of these stocks are in government hands. IEA countries hold more than ==1.2 billion barrels of public stocks==, and about 600 million more barrels are kept by oil companies because the law requires them to [3].

In a crisis, the IEA can launch a "collective action". Member countries meet, assess how much oil is missing from the market, then jointly decide on a volume to release [3]. Each government then chooses how to provide its share.

There are two main ways. First, the state sells or lends oil from its own reserves. Second, it ==lowers the minimum stock imposed on companies==, which can then sell what they were holding in reserve. In March 2022, more than two-thirds of the effort came from public stocks, and nearly a third from lower company obligations [4].
Japan used this second lever in 2026: it cut the mandatory stock of its refiners and traders from 70 to 55 days, allowing them to put that oil back on the market [13].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.2: In France: tanks paid for at the pump
A fraction of a cent per litre, for several months of insurance.
In France, the law requires oil operators to keep strategic stocks at all times. The volume is set at ==29.5% of the quantities sold the previous year==, or about 108 days of sales [7].

Two bodies handle it. The Professional Committee for Strategic Petroleum Stocks (CPSSP), tasked since a 1992 law with financing the system, and SAGESS, a company set up at the initiative of oil firms, which buys, sells and stores on behalf of the CPSSP [6].

In total, France keeps ==about 16 million tonnes of hydrocarbons==, two-thirds of which are held by SAGESS [6]. Before MPs in April 2026, its CEO put the country's actual level at between 100 and 110 days [7].

Who pays? You do, a little, every time you fill up. The costs are borne by fuel distributors, without going through the state budget, and managing the stocks costs ==about 0.75 cents per litre== [7]. A drop in the final price, but over billions of litres, it pays for millions of tonnes in reserve.

These stocks were bought over the years, sometimes long ago. According to the Prime Minister's office, the diesel released in October 2026 had been acquired at ==€0.28 per litre==, while the market was then paying €1.10 [6]. That is what makes it possible to sell it at cost while bringing prices down.

Storing crude oil is not enough: in a crisis, you still need refineries to turn it into petrol, diesel or jet fuel. If they are hit, or if the country mostly imports already-refined fuels, crude is of little use.

That is why the European Union requires at least 30 days of stocks, or a third of the obligation, to be held as refined products [5]. In 2022, the public stocks released were mostly crude, while lowering company obligations mostly freed up finished products [4].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.3: Elsewhere: salt domes, Japanese records and Chinese secrecy
Each country stores in its own way, depending on its geology, its dependence and its secrets.

The American reserve is the best known. The oil sits in ==caverns carved out of salt== at four sites on the Gulf Coast: Bryan Mound and Big Hill in Texas, West Hackberry and Bayou Choctaw in Louisiana. Its capacity is about 713.5 million barrels, and it can deliver up to 4.4 million barrels a day for 90 days before the rate starts to fall [9].

This reserve has been used a lot in recent years. In spring 2022, Washington announced a sale of 180 million barrels, the largest in its history; in October, the stock fell to 405 million barrels, its lowest level since 1984 [10]. In 2026, a new agreement provides for 172 million barrels to be released: in early October, only ==283 million barrels== remained, the lowest level since October 1982 [11].

Japan, which imports almost all its oil, chose to be the best protected. At the end of 2025, it held ==254 days of consumption==, or 470 million barrels: 146 days in state stocks, 101 days with private companies and 7 days in joint stocks with producing countries [13].
In March 2026, Tokyo announced its largest-ever release: 45 days of consumption, nearly 20% of its reserves. The previous record, 25 days, dated from the 2011 earthquake and tsunami [13].

China does not publish its figures. The US Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates its stocks reached ==nearly 1.4 billion barrels== at the end of 2025, counting the commercial stocks that state companies must keep for emergencies. The share held directly by the state is thought to be about 360 million barrels [14].

Beijing built up this oil very quickly: about 1.1 million barrels a day on average in 2025, according to the same estimate [14]. But without official figures, it is hard to know when and how China draws on its reserves.
Salt domes form watertight caverns, dug by dissolving the salt with fresh water, which can be enlarged if needed [9]. It is far cheaper than building steel tanks for hundreds of millions of barrels.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.4: "For the first time", the stocks are being used to protect purchasing power. Roland Lescure, French Economy Minister, October 2026 [7].

IEA collective actions are rare. Before 2026, there had been only five: the Gulf War in 1991, Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the war in Libya in 2011, and twice in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine [3].

In 2022, IEA countries first decided, on 1 March, to release 60 million barrels; in the end they made nearly 62.7 million available. On 1 April, they added 120 million. In total, ==182.7 million barrels==, about three-quarters of which came from public stocks [4].

Then came 2026. With the war in the Middle East, exports of crude and fuels through the Strait of Hormuz fell to ==less than 10% of their pre-conflict level==. On 11 March, the 32 IEA countries unanimously decided to put 400 million barrels on the market, more than twice the 2022 total [3].

That was not enough to ease the diesel shortage. On 2 October 2026, the G7 agreed to release another 100 million barrels of diesel and crude over four months, with ==a large share of diesel in the first 20 days== [15].

France is doing its part. The government is releasing 10 million barrels of diesel, about one-fifth of the diesel SAGESS held at the end of 2024 [7]. They are sold at cost to distributors, split according to their 2025 market shares, from 28 October, in an operation lasting three months, from November to January [8].

This is a change in nature. These stocks were meant to prevent a physical shortage. In 2026, they are also being used, ==for the first time in France, to lower the price paid at the pump==, as the Economy Minister pointed out [7].
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.5: Does it really bring prices down?
A stock buys time. It does not reopen a strait.

The effects are real but modest. After the big US sale of 2022, the US Treasury estimated it had lowered petrol prices ==by 13 to 31 cents per gallon== (about 3.8 litres), while acknowledging that it is not known exactly how much of the fall in crude prices reached the pump [12].

The market reacts mostly to announcements. After the G7 decision of 2 October 2026, Brent fell 1.48% to $100.8 a barrel [15]. A real drop, but a small one compared with the surge caused by the Hormuz crisis.

In France, the government hopes for a drop of ==12 to 18 cents per litre of diesel==, or about ten euros saved per fill-up on average. The head of TotalEnergies expects more like 8 to 12 cents in his network [8].

The limit is physical: a stock is finite. In Japan, one analyst sums it up: these reserves stabilise prices in the short term, but they ==mainly buy time== and cannot offset a long disruption at Hormuz [13].

Each release also weakens the next line of defence. In the United States, the reserve is at its lowest since 1982 [11]. If a new crisis broke out tomorrow, there would be fewer barrels left to respond.
culture.reserves-strategiques.sections.6: The debates: cost, political use, transition
Insurance you pay for every year, and hesitate to use.

First debate: cost. Storing millions of tonnes ties up money, tanks and caverns, for oil that is almost never used. In France, the bill goes through the pump price [7]; in the United States, the reserve belongs to the federal government [9]. Its supporters reply that this is the price of insurance.

Second debate: what should these stocks be used for? For some, only real supply disruptions. For others, they can also cushion a price spike. France's use in October 2026, presented as a purchasing-power measure, revived this question [7]. The head of SAGESS had pointed out in April that these were "not sales" but loans to be returned; the government says a sale remains legally possible [6].

Third debate: refilling. An emptied stock must be bought back, ideally when prices are low. In the United States, the administration now offers to ==lend oil to companies==, 40 million barrels in its latest offer, rather than sell it [11]. Japan, for its part, must rebuild reserves it drew down heavily in 2026 [13].

Fourth debate: the energy transition. If countries consume less oil, their imports fall, and the 90-day rule mechanically requires smaller stocks. But as long as lorries, planes and tractors run on diesel and jet fuel, dependence remains high, especially for refined products.

Finally, oil is no longer the only energy stored as a precaution. Gas is also stored before winter, under other rules. For you, the lesson is concrete: when a crisis breaks out far away, part of what happens at the petrol station depends on tanks and caverns you will never see.
culture.reserves-strategiques.didYouKnow: France's 2026 stock release is not only for motorists: it also covers off-road diesel used by farmers and construction firms, as well as heating oil, and more than 300 rural petrol stations are receiving support [8].
